claims.text: An operator pairs custom resources with a controller that follows the control loop to manage one application, encoding in software what a human operator of that application does by hand.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io Concepts > Extend Kubernetes > Operator pattern (overview, Motivation, Operators in Kubernetes)

claims.text: Each pass of a controller's loop reads the desired state (the custom resource) and the current state through the API server and acts to bring the current state closer to the desired one.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io Concepts > Cluster Architecture > Controllers (Controller pattern; Design); refs/kubernetes-website .../architecture/controller.md

claims.text: Because a controller built this way compares states rather than replaying a list of changes, a change it missed (for instance while its Pod restarted) still shows as a difference when it next compares and is acted on then.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io Controllers > Desired versus current state; Design ('Controllers can fail'); outline item 2

claims.text: After the Secret api-tls named by Certificate api-cert is deleted, cert-manager, told nothing, issues a new certificate into a Secret of the same name, type kubernetes.io/tls, with a different serial number.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/operator.txt lines 1-6; scripts/k8s/operator.sh lines 10-31 @ stage-3; cert-manager.io Concepts > Certificate (issuance triggers)

claims.text: cert-manager records each signing for a Certificate as a CertificateRequest (in this lab api-cert-2) and by default keeps one per Certificate (revisionHistoryLimit default 1), removing older ones; after the reissue only api-cert-2 (issuer lab-ca, Ready True) is listed.
claims.source_hint: cert-manager.io API reference > CertificateSpec.revisionHistoryLimit; outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/operator.txt lines 8-10; operator.sh lines 27-30 @ stage-3

claims.text: The Certificate spec names only secretName api-tls, dnsNames donhang.localhost and issuerRef kind Issuer name lab-ca; it states no signing steps.

operator.sh runs cert-manager.sh only if api-cert does not exist, then waits for Ready; stores the serial in before, read by serial() with openssl; after the delete polls for the Secret once a second up to 60 times, creating nothing; show prints then runs a command.
RBAC permissions are purely additive, with no deny rules, so a controller's ServiceAccount may act only on the objects, verbs and namespaces that some rule bound to it grants.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io Reference > Using RBAC Authorization (Role and ClusterRole: 'Permissions are purely additive'); refs .../access-authn-authz/rbac.md line 58

claims.text: kubectl auth can-i list secrets -A answers yes for system:serviceaccount:cert-manager:cert-manager and no for operator-lessons:default; the same cert-manager controller ClusterRole also grants get, watch, create, update and delete on secrets.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/operator.txt lines 12-15; deploy/cert-manager/cert-manager.yaml lines 12505-12514 (controller ClusterRole, secrets verbs)

claims.text: A Pod whose manifest names no ServiceAccount runs as the ServiceAccount named default in its namespace.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io Concepts > Security > Service Accounts (default service accounts); Configure Service Accounts for Pods

claims.text: Because its ServiceAccount may read Secrets in every namespace, a bug in cert-manager or an upgrade that brings one can reach every Secret in the cluster, not only those it wrote.
claims.source_hint: follows from claim 9; kubernetes.io Operator pattern; RBAC Good Practices (least privilege)

claims.text: A PostgreSQL operator can take on keeping standbys, switching to one on failure and taking backups on a schedule, driven by a custom resource that describes the database.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io Operator pattern > An example operator (SampleDB: StatefulSet, backups, upgrades); outline item 4

claims.text: An operator fits when its project is maintained, with fixes for the Kubernetes versions you run, and your team learns how it behaves; otherwise an incident means debugging the database and someone else's automation together.
claims.source_hint: outline item 6; contrast k8s.l2.database-in-the-cluster (managed database option)

claims.text: PostgreSQL streaming replication is asynchronous by default: the primary confirms a commit without waiting for the standby to receive it, so a standby can trail by its replication lag and those writes can be lost on failover.
claims.source_hint: PostgreSQL 17 docs 26.2.5 Streaming Replication; 26.2.8 Synchronous Replication

claims.text: An operator usually brings a controller, often run as a Deployment, and RBAC rights besides its CRDs; cert-manager's pinned manifest (v1.20.4) has three Deployments and six CRDs.
claims.source_hint: deploy/cert-manager/cert-manager.yaml @ stage-3 (kind: Deployment x3, CustomResourceDefinition x6); kubernetes.io Operator pattern > Deploying operators
